To predetermine something means to decide, settle, or establish it before the relevant event, process, or moment actually takes place.

Think of it in two parts: pre- means before, and determine means to decide something conclusively. So predetermine = to decide in advance.

"Determine" simply means to decide or settle something. "Predetermine" adds a crucial layer of timing — the decision happens before the process that would normally produce that decision.

Compare:

  • "The judge determined the verdict." → The judge decided after hearing the case. Normal.
  • "The judge predetermined the verdict." → The judge had already decided before the trial began — before hearing a single word of evidence.

That second sentence signals something is deeply wrong. The trial was just a performance. The real decision had already been made.

That gap — between the hidden earlier decision and the process that pretended to produce it — is exactly what "predetermine" captures.
Who or what can predetermine something?

1. A person or group with power
Anyone with the authority to control outcomes — a committee, a boss, a corrupt official, a government — can predetermine results. "The committee predetermined who would win the contract before the bidding even opened." The bidding process was theater.

2. God or a higher power (in religious/theological discussions)
Many religious traditions hold that God has predetermined certain events or even individual fates. In Calvinist Christian theology, for example, the doctrine of predestination holds that God predetermined before the creation of the world which souls would be saved. This is one of the most debated ideas in Christian theology — because if God predetermined your fate, what role does your own choice play?

3. Fate, physics, or the universe (in philosophy)
Some philosophers argue that everything in the universe — every event, every thought, every "choice" — was predetermined by prior causes, stretching back to the very beginning of time. Each event causes the next, in a chain that was set in motion long before you were born. This view is called predeterminism (or hard determinism), and it raises a deeply uncomfortable question: if everything is predetermined, do humans have any real free will at all?

4. Biology and nature
Nature or genetics can predetermine traits and tendencies. "Certain genetic conditions predetermine a person's risk of developing heart disease." Here, predetermine means that the outcome was "decided" by your biology before you were even born, before any lifestyle choice you made.

5. Rules, criteria, or systems established in advance
Organizations and researchers often predetermine their methods, standards, or criteria as part of careful planning. "The panel predetermined the grading rubric before reviewing any applications." This is methodical and responsible — done to avoid bias.
The range of contexts — and how the word feels in each

In everyday life — usually negative and suspicious:
When someone says a result was "predetermined" in ordinary conversation — an election, a competition, a job interview, a court verdict — they almost always mean it was rigged. The process that took place (the vote, the contest, the interviews) was a hollow formality, because the real decision had been made behind closed doors before any of it started.

"Everyone knew the election was predetermined — the ruling party had already decided who would win."

It implies unfairness, manipulation, and betrayal of trust.

In science and research — usually neutral or even positive:
Researchers are actually encouraged to predetermine their hypotheses, measurements, and success criteria before running experiments. This practice, called pre-registration, is considered excellent scientific conduct because it prevents researchers from unconsciously adjusting their methods after seeing the data to get a desired result.

"The team predetermined their evaluation criteria before the clinical trial began, ensuring unbiased results."

Here, predetermining is responsible, not sinister.

In philosophy and theology — serious and weighty:
Predetermine touches on some of the most profound questions humans have ever asked: Does God control fate? Do the laws of physics leave any room for genuine choice? Is your life already "written"? The word carries the full weight of centuries of debate.

"If God predetermines all events, then human freedom becomes very difficult to explain."

One of the most important things to understand about "predetermine" is an implication it almost always carries: if something is predetermined, then whatever happens in between may be meaningless.

If a competition's winner was predetermined, the competition itself doesn't matter. If a trial's verdict was predetermined, the presentation of evidence doesn't matter. If your fate is predetermined, your choices don't matter. This is why the word so often feels either ominous (in everyday life), philosophically unsettling (in debates about free will), or carefully reassuring (in research, where removing that "in-between noise" is exactly the goal).

You will encounter "predetermine" most often in its passive form:

  • "The outcome was predetermined."
  • "The result had been predetermined long before we arrived."
  • "Success in this system is essentially predetermined by the family you're born into."

This passive form emphasizes that the decision was already in place — without necessarily naming who made it. It focuses your attention on the fait accompli: the thing was already decided, and the process after was secondary.

• "The winner of the reality show was predetermined — producers had already chosen the finalist weeks before the public voted." (rigged outcome)
  • "Some theologians believe God predetermines the salvation of certain individuals regardless of their deeds." (theological predestination)
  • "Stoic philosophers argued that the entire course of the universe was predetermined from the moment of its creation." (philosophical predeterminism)
  • "The committee predetermined eligibility requirements before the scholarship cycle opened, to ensure fairness." (advance planning — neutral/positive)
  • "Scientists have found that genetic factors predetermine an individual's likelihood of developing certain conditions." (natural/biological)
  • "She felt her future in that company was predetermined — no matter how well she performed, she'd never be promoted." (feeling of inevitability, powerlessness)

To predetermine something is to decide what it will be before the process, event, or moment that would naturally have produced that decision — and this prior decision makes everything that comes after either a formality, a performance, a fixed destiny, or a carefully controlled starting point, depending on the context.
